speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. Rural post offices are the lifeline of the community. Farmers and ranchers depend on the post office for mail-order service for garden seeds, clothing, and so on. It has been brought to my attention that telephones are being removed from rural post offices in my constituency. Therefore, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Stewart):
That the Post Office stop any further removal of telephones from rural post offices as many rural folk use the telephone to determine whether parcels have arrived rather than driving to town and wasting fuel.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, I ask for the unanimous consent of the House to introduce a motion dealing with an important matter of pressing necessity.
Following the flat refusal of the Minister of Finance to accept the decision of the Quebec government concerning the removal of the sales tax for a year in weak economic areas; since the dictatorial move of the federal Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) is giving Quebecers further proof of his oneway negotiations with Quebec, when the exclusive responsibilities of the provinces guaranteed by the constitution are involved and following many telephone calls from Quebec taxpayers protesting against this unhealthy intrusion of the federal government to prevent Quebecers from setting their own priorities; and considering the grave danger of deepening further the differences between Quebec and Ottawa, which would be the worst threat to Canadian harmony, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Allard):
That the Minister of Finance reconsider and accept for once the decision of Quebec which wants to act alone within its own jurisdiction.

INCREASE IN SALES TAX AFTER SIX-MONTH PERIOD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. In view of the very clear feeling on the part of the western premiers that federal-provincial relations have been damaged by this experience, and in view of the Prime Minister's having stated just now that the federal government is prepared to do something to try to repair that damage, may I put this proposition to him: In view of the fact that the federal government is taking full credit for the reductions which will now take place in the sales tax of the various provinces, will the federal government-if it is still there six months from now-use all of its capacity to effect the news and to tell us what is going on; will it use that to make it clear to the people of Canada, when the sales tax goes back up six months from now, that the responsibility for it is that of the federal government?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: INCREASE IN SALES TAX AFTER SIX-MONTH PERIOD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the position of the government on the budget is very simple. We gave room to the provinces to increase their income tax and cut their sales tax. This was done by depriving ourselves of federal tax funds, or federal funds from income tax. We decided to do this for a period of six months. In six months, presumably, when this ends, we will have to increase the taxes again to what they were. The people of Canada will know to whom they are paying taxes, unless we decide then to have another budget. They will know that.
In so far as the position of the premiers is concerned, I repeat what I said earlier: they, through the ministers of finance, accepted this proposition. They discussed it over a period of several weeks. I find it passing strange now that the premiers, not the ministers of finance, are saying there has not been co-operation. If the premiers feel that, I am prepared to see them. Let them come to Ottawa next week and I will make an appointment with them. I would be glad to discuss with them what budgetary processes they would like to establish in the future.
Oral Questions
Here is a proposal in which the federal government said to the provincial governments, "We will both put some money in. The federal government will put in more than you. We will put some money in, and we will reduce sales taxes to the Canadian people in order to stimulate effective demand in the economy." And the finance ministers of the provinces accepted. They were not forced to do that; they could have said no, just as one province refused to give an answer. But no. Obviously there is some lack of communication between the ministers of finance and the premiers-the left hand does not know what the right hand is doing-and now they are complaining.
There could not have been a better attempt by the federal government to co-operate with the provinces in putting together a budget with which they agreed. The Minister of Finance travelled across the country to do that; he travelled across the country meeting the finance ministers of the provinces. After three weeks of consultations, we arrived at a budget with which nine provinces agreed and the other remained silent. I now find it passing strange that they are having second thoughts and playing politics to help the Leader of the Opposition.

subsubtopic: COMMITAL OF DANGEROUS OFFENDERS UNDER "HOSPITAL ORDERS"
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this bill is premised on the acknowledgment of the fact that because brutal "justice" is frequently meted out by fellow inmates to child molesters, judges hesitate to sentence these offenders to prison terms. By granting special power to the criminal courts to make "hospital orders" as opposed to usual terms of imprisonment, this bill is designed to provide needed medical treatment to offenders suffering from psychopathic disorders and, especially important, to protect the public from the risk of further offences being committed if the offenders are at large.
Motion agreed to, bill read the first time and ordered to be printed.

FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE The House resumed, from Thursday, April 13, consideration of the motion by Mr. Chretien that this House approves in general the budgetary policy of the government, and the amendment of Mr. Stevens (p. 4439).

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert K. Andras (President of the Treasury Board):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I rise to take a few brief moments to enter this debate, I begin by expressing my congratulations to my col-

April 14, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Andras
league, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien), both for the budget he presented on April 10 and for the way he is handling what I think anyone on any side of the House or anywhere in the country would recognize as a very difficult portfolio in admittedly difficult times of economic tension.
I believe it is a reasonable assessment to say that the general reaction across the country to the budget of the other night has been favourable. It is obviously correct to say it has not met with total acceptance by our friends across the floor. That is understandable, because they are the opposition. It would be a great surprise to see any measure presented by the government with which they could find favour, even if there were some elements of it they could find in their hearts to accept.
We have heard in response to the budget that it was too little, that it was half measures. The Progressive Conservatives stated they would have cut taxes by over $2 billion. Indeed, that becomes the option game for the Canadian people. They have said that the budget is short term, it is the wrong thing to do, and so on.
I would like to take a few minutes to put on the record the cumulative measures and the impact on the year 1978 in terms of tax reductions and the cumulative measures taken by this government over a period of time, most recently on April 10 with the cooperation of at least nine of the provinces. That was a phenomenal step forward in federal-provincial relations, despite the criticisms some members opposite have addressed to the one aberration, that is, the decision of the province of Quebec.
It was a step forward in federal-provincial cooperation on fiscal-economic matters. It fell very well into what I consider to be a very significant advance between the provinces and the federal government which took place at the first ministers' conference a month or so ago. At that time, nearly all the senior leaders of various levels of government met and, for whatever the reason, reached general agreement on a set of principles that were well enunciated and will be beneficial to Canada.
I return to the cumulative stimulus in the economy of tax reductions resulting from actions taken by this government over a period of time. In 1978 the total effective tax reductions from those actions will be $4,497 million. If anyone says that is a half measure, they are playing the option game with the Canadian economy. That would be totally irresponsible in some of the measures they are suggesting. Let me detail where that $4,497 million comes from.
On the personal income tax side, the automatic indexation that was introduced three years ago, which is casually dismissed on many occasions by members opposite, amounted to an effective $850 million personal tax reduction as of January 1 and continuing through the year.
The carry-on effect of the personal tax reductions in 1978 of the March 31, 1977, budget measures is another $675 million tax reduction this year on the personal income tax side. The measures taken by my colleague, the Minister of Finance, on
October 20 last represent another tax reduction on the personal tax side of $730 million.
On the personal income tax side, in a measure which is considered to stimulate spending and alleviate the effect of inflation, particularly on lower income families, the total tax reduction effective January, 1978, amounted to $2,255 million. That is not a half measure.
The effective tax reduction flowing from the retail sales tax reduction announced on April 10 is $1,147 million, which will be put directly into consumer spending because it cannot be realized unless people buy things and take advantage of the tax reduction.
On the corporation tax side, the cumulative effect of 1978 taxes to be paid by corporations, will be a total reduction, as a result of action taken by the government, of $1,095 million. On March 31, 1977, the then minister of finance introduced in his budget certain adjustments in inventory tax measures and also announced the provision of investment tax credits. Those two measures combined amount to tax cuts for corporations of $895 million in this fiscal year. On October 20 the Minister of Finance announced access for corporations to employment tax credit and this, if used in the current year, will amount to another $100 million tax relief to the corporations.
In addition, on April 10, the other night, the Minister of Finance provided access to a higher level of write-off in connection with research and development which will amount to approximately $50 million this year. He also provided concessions in taxation applied to tertiary oil and other areas amounting to $50 million. So we are looking at a corporate tax reduction effective this year of $1,095 million, and at a total of tax reductions effective in 1978 of approximately $4,497 million. Mr. Speaker, I do not think those who talk about that as a half measure are acting responsibly or even in a credible fashion.
There has also been an attempt to say that this is the wrong way to go-that this is not part of a planned economic approach. I submit that this view is not the correct one. The personal income tax cuts, the income tax cuts, the corporations tax cuts to which I have referred, do focus not only on the short term but also on the medium and longer term. Certainly they are concerned with helping lower income people-I refer particularly to the personal tax cuts and to the retail sales tax reductions.
I would also point out that the April 10 measure especially deals directly with the stimulating of consumer demand-we are all concerned about the question of unused capacity in our plants resulting from an apparent reluctance to purchase goods-thereby stimulating further expansion and employment. That is the purpose of the retail tax deductions which took effect the other day. Their purpose was to stimulate consumer spending so as to absorb some of that unutilized capacity and thereby trigger the other measures taken by the government which address themselves to the medium and the long term, and, if I may say so, to structural problems as well.

April 14, 1978

What else is investment tax credit but investment in the medium and the long term growth of the economy? That is its purpose, to encourage people to invest in industrial and commercial activity, a process which will, in the end, result in the creation of more jobs. The inventory adjustment measure addresses itself to structural problems and to the medium and the long term. The employment tax credits are addressed directly to the reduction of unemployment through the stimulation of business activity and confidence. What else is the $50 million which is going into research and development-I hope it turns out to be more-but an investment in the medium and the long term and in the structural aspects to which we all wish to address ourselves?
Those who criticize this budget or the actions of the government for not addressing the deeper problems, had better tell me what else the tax reductions made the other night in the tertiary oil field and rail transportation are, what else are they but investment in the structure of our society which, we say, troubles us.
Finally, the change in the tax measures applied to family and corporate farms will also encourage our food producers.
Keeping all these things in mind, I submit that those who argue that government policy lacks continuity, lacks symmetry, lacks an over-all strategy, are failing, either deliberately or through lack of understanding, to give credit to the cumulative effect of all the measures which have been taken.
I intend, now, to make a statement which I think is indisputable but which may surprise some people. One hears from certain businessmen and others that they face a punitive corporate tax regime in Canada. That is not the case. The Canadian corporate tax structure is as favourable as that of any country in the world, including the United States. This was the case before the measures taken the other day, and the position of the corporations has now been enhanced by the concessions I have detailed. I think it is time for people to stop talking about how they are being punished and handicapped and inhibited when operating businesses in this country. The facts show that this is not the case.
One often hears from certain businessmen that they are over-regulated, that they are being hamstrung by the number of regulations with which they are obliged to conform, the amount of information they are called to supply, and so on. Let those people go down to the United States, into any state of the union, and start to operate under the much harsher regulatory regime applied there, and then tell us we are not competitive in that field.
The other side of the budget picture involves the question of fiscal responsibility. We have heard a constant stream of unreal statements from the opposition to the effect that no real restraint in expenditure is being shown by the government. I am glad to recognize that this is not believed by people who analyze the situation seriously. It is really nothing but a political statement, because the facts are indisputable.
Governments, not just the federal government but all the governments in this country-and thank goodness for that-
The Budget-Mr. Andras
have turned away from the admittedly excessive spending of the last ten or 12 years, which culminated in a bite on the economy by all levels of government of about 40 per cent. Incidentally, one hears the figure of 42 per cent as the figure for spending by all governments. That is not correct. National statistics clearly indicate that it was in fact 39.9 per cent-I don't know where these people are getting their statistics. At any rate, government expenditures are now declining from the peak of 1975. The same statistics show that the reduction as a percentage of the gross national product is taking place mainly at the federal level through the exercise of restraint in federal spending.
What is the story of our expenditure levels in the last three years? Two or three years ago we began to set out publicly what our total spending would be for the coming fiscal year. That had not been done before by any government, to my knowledge. We set out our commitment and said that we would not exceed it. We said that our objective was to restrain budgetary and non-budgetary increases, capital and non-capital spending, and total cash spending, to something less than the growth in the gross national product.
Our first commitment of a dollar figure ceiling was for the year 1976-77. Our original publicly stated and committed spending target was $42.15 billion. We actually spent $1 billion less than that in fiscal year 1976-77. We spent $41,078 billion. We stated our commitment and met it. Our percentage increase year on year was 10.2 per cent.
In 1977-78 we started off by making the same move. We laid out publicly and in this House what our total spending ceiling would be for fiscal year 1977-78. When I tabled the main estimates for that year on February 16, 1977, I stated that we would contain ourselves to a ceiling of $45.1 billion. Shortly thereafter, in cooperation with the then minister of finance and to provide an offset of expenditure reduction to enable him to make certain tax cuts which we all thought were then required, we reduced that spending target, again publicly. The then minister of finance stated in his budget speech of March 31 that spending would be $44.45 billion, a cut then of $650 million.
For the statement of the Minister of Finance of April 10- and I was glad to be able to do this; I had much cooperation from many people-I was able to tell him that we would come $200 million under that downward revised ceiling of expenditures for 1977-78, and in fact I am saying that we will be in, at, or under $44.25 billion rather than $44.45 billion. That will represent a 7.7 per cent increase over the previous year, which is very close to or even a little under the inflation rate for that year, and which means that we contained ourselves to no real growth at all in our expenditures for the fiscal year just ended.
Taking the same tactics again-and I think these are eminently responsible-when the Minister of Finance, in conjunction with his colleagues and in co-operation with the provinces, made the basic decision to cut retail sales taxes, provide research and development assistance, and so forth, the other

April 14, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Andras
day, we consulted. We said that there should be some kind of offset to the reduction of revenue inherent in those tax cuts to the federal treasury. The $1,147 billion of retail tax cuts plus the research and development tax cut and the tertiary oil and railway development tax cuts will end up costing in revenue to the federal government about $900 million.
Everybody knows we have a deficit and that we are concerned about it, and, of course, the provinces are sharing in that over-all tax reduction. However, for those who might have been concerned about the result and the effect on our cash requirements this year of that $900 million federal investment in tax reductions, the arithmetic is that with the $200 million under-spending for 1977-78 which I was able to announce, and with the commitment to cut another $350 million off our spending total for 1978-79, we will have offset that $900 million revenue reduction by a $550 million expenditure reduction. That means that there might be a net increase in our deficit as a result of the budget measures the other night of about $350 million. That $350 million will result in the stimulation of consumer demand.
There will be a $1,147 billion retail sales tax reduction, and there will be another $100 million in other structural tax encouragement for corporations. I think it was an eminently responsible budget. We recognized the limitations in our fiscal situation by virtue of high cash requirements, and we offset those to the maximum by about $550 million. I can assure hon. members that that $350 million expenditure reduction to which we are committed will be met, and I submit the track record of 1976-77 and 1977-78 as evidence that when we make that commitment we will make that expenditure reduction.
Hear, hear!

As we do that we are reducing the reserve for supplementary estimates, which I detailed when I presented the main estimates on February 22, by that $350 million. I am not going to say that this will be an easy job for the government. I know from the experience of a year and a half in my present portfolio that it will not be easy for me.
We will have to deny submissions for new programs. We will have to cut back in some other programs. That will be difficult. Just saying, as the opposition does, that if it had the reins of power it would cut expenditures by $2 billion just like that, will not deceive the Canadian public. The Canadian public will not be deceived by that kind of nonsense. I would like very much to hear from what level the opposition would cut, and precisely where. We have been doing it. I would like to know what programs the opposition would attack. Whose ox are they going to gore? It is not an easy job.
Members of the opposition say that if they had power, they would cut taxes by $2 billion in addition to the $4,497 billion which I have delineated. They would cut expenditures by $2 billion just like that, but they really do not know what they are talking about. They have left no precision on the record as to where the money would come from or how they would do it.
My time is limited. There are one or two corrections I want to make. I want to correct some of the rather loose things the

hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) threw around the other day. He claimed that instead of the expenditure reduction I am telling the House we are accomplishing, our expenditures for 1977-78 were more than $1 billion more than had been forecast in the budget speech of March 31, 1977. I have already dealt with that. I will forgive the hon. member by saying that he probably took the wrong line from the book. Whether that was convenience or not, I do not know, but it was the wrong line, and therefore a distortion of the facts when the hon. member said that total spending was up.
I will forgive him for that, but there was another rather puzzling set of figures the hon. member used when he attacked the government for growth in the number in the federal public service. He said that in 1968 when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) came to power there were 280,000 people in the total federal public service and that, as of the end of 1977, that number had grown to 580,000.
When the hon. member gave a figure for the base year 1968, he quoted the figure 280,000, conveniently leaving out the Armed Forces and all employees of Crown corporations. If he had included those employees, the base figure would have been 470,000. He conveniently left those employees out of the base year figure, but somehow they all turned up in the figure for the comparative year of 1977, 580,000. I am not sure whether that was because of poor research or because of absolutely blatant chicanery.
The latter.

Again I will say that the hon. member probably took the wrong page or the wrong line, but he should not make statements like that and expect to be believed in everything else he says. It is curious that his errors are always in the wrong direction.
We are achieving restraint in the growth of the federal public service. We have chosen, in the expenditure pattern and those kinds of things, to do it on a responsible, gradual basis, because we want to direct it downward. We do not want to take Draconian measures today which could have a very serious impact on the economy later.
There is a tendency in these debates to throw statistics around. I did it because I felt I had to correct some of the very, very bad information that has been put out in this debate by members opposite.
I want to wind up my remarks, Mr. Speaker, with this point. Nobody realistically would say that in this country we are making economic progress. Nobody is saying that and nobody is failing to recognize, except in the heat of rhetorical debate and political opportunism, that many of the problems we have in this country are absolutely, correctly, and factually shared in most of the western world. We share those problems, and there is no amount of bombastic rhetoric that will convince people that we can isolate our situation from that in the rest of the world.
April 14, 1978

I have great faith in the mass wisdom of people in this country, and faith in their understanding that the world is facing economic tensions and that there is confusion. Even those countries we tout as having the best economies in the world are facing economic tensions. Helmut Schmidt is reported as having said the other day to a friend of his that he is totally puzzled about how the economy of the world is operating today. There is nobody who will stand before the electorate and say, "We have all the answers, we have the miracle wand to wave and, if you just trust us, all the problems will be solved". There are some people who will try to convey that, if they had the reins of power, all the problems in the world would be solved, but I do not think Canadians would be fooled about that.
In the process of overkill, of the constant verbal barrage of gloom, doom, and disaster, always talking about the negatives in our society and in our economy, and never admitting or playing up or putting into the balance the positive aspects of our economy which still in our country far outweigh the negatives, I question what consideration is being given to the psychological confidence of Canadians. So on that basis I look across the floor and I question, not only the matter of policy responsibility but also the question of psychological responsibility, when what we need in this country above all, and indeed in the western world, is an emphasis on the positive, a recognition that this country stands economically, socially, in terms of justice, and in terms of any indicator you want to look at, as one of the most favoured nations in the world. The only way in which we could louse that up is by an overkill of opportunistic negativism, which prevails in this House all too often and obviously in the press.
We really have nothing to fear but fear itself. I think it is time we faced our problems realistically. It is time we patched up our weaknesses, we recognized that things are being done, and we recognized that governments alone cannot do them but that the decisions of businessmen, unions and individuals in this country are collectively far more important than what we think we are doing here in the House. If we have a role to play as political leaders and public figures, it is one of presenting a balanced picture, and today I say what we need is a balanced picture that comes out positive and not negative.
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mr. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we meet to debate this budget in an air of crisis, and there is a crisis in this country, a very serious economic crisis. All we have to do is to examine what has taken place in this country in the three days following the bringing down of the budget by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien). No sooner was the budget brought down than the unemployment figures were released the following day by Statistics Canada showing a substantial increase in the rate of unemployment in this country. The rate of unemployment rose to 8.6 per cent, a rise of three points over the previous month, putting 1,045,000 Canadians in the ranks of the unemployed.
The Budget-Mr. McGrath
As if that was not bad enough, we had the consumer price index released on the following day showing another substantial increase in the rate of inflation, which is now running at 8.8 per cent, an increase in one month of 1.1 per cent.
In the midst of all this we had an unprecedented fall in the Canadian dollar. Our dollar is sinking daily in response to the minister's budget, demonstrating beyond any doubt that the international financial community have no confidence in this government's ability to manage the Canadian economy. Certainly they have demonstrated that they have no confidence in the budget brought down last Monday night by the Minister of Finance. Today, the Canadian dollar is trading at less than 87 cents.
Shame!

It is still sinking. By the weekend it will be down to 86 cents, and we are just a few days away from an 85 cent dollar and all it means to Canada, to the Canadian economy, to Canadian consumers, and to our rate of inflation, closely tied as we are to the U.S. economy, with our pricing system geared to the U.S. dollar.
And yet we have the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) standing in his place today trying to justify the unjustifiable. He threw out a few challenges. I pity the President of the Treasury Board. He has a very difficult role to play; he has an impossible task. He criticized my colleague, the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens), and he criticized my leader. He criticized this party for daring to advocate $2 billion worth of tax cuts, and he challenged us to identify them. I thought that the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Clark) did just that when he spoke in this debate in one of the great speeches of the House of Commons.
Hear, hear!

I am sorry the President of the Treasury Board could not wait for a reply to his question. We can identify where $2 billion could be saved in this country. We are spending almost that much on consultants' fees, which is a euphemistic term for patronage. We are spending almost $2 billion on consultants' fees, notwithstanding the fact that we have built up in this country a substantial body of experts within the Public Service of Canada capable of meeting just about any challenge presented to them by any department of government. We have a highly trained, highly competent Public Service in this country, yet we go outside of the Public Service every day, every week, and every month, and spend almost $2 billion annually on consultants' fees. That is where we can make the saving right there. That is some of the fat we would trim from the government.
My leader spoke about sunset laws, about bringing the curtain down on some of the redundant Crown corporations which are no longer relevant. We have a ridiculous situation today where the government hardly knows how many Crown corporations it has under its jurisdiction. Certainly the curtain should be brought down on some of these redundant Crown corporations, and the remainder should be made more

April 14, 1978
The Budget-Mr. McGrath
accountable to parliament so that their budgets can be kept within control. As it stands now, they answer to no one. In fact they are accountable to no one, as has been demonstrated by the experiences of the past year with at least two Crown corporations dealing in the commercial world.
When the government took office ten years ago, the total budget was about the extent of what is the total anticipated deficit of the government this year. That is where we are. That is the consequence of the disarray arising from the financial mismanagement of the Canadian economy. The former minister of finance originally forecast a $7.2 billion budgetary deficit for 1978. Some seven months later, the present Minister of Finance said that the deficit would be $9.2 billion. The 1978 accounts will show a budgetary deficit of $10.3 billion, which is 43 per cent greater than the original forecast and comparable to the total amount of the government's budget when it took office ten years ago. That is the setting we find ourselves in for this debate today.
Our annual rate of inflation is the second worst of the major industrialized countries of the west, 8.8 per cent. That is the climate we are in, as we come into the post controls period which commences tomorrow. The government does not have a post control strategy to cope with this new round of inflation, which is being influenced directly by the dollar crisis.
What do we have in terms of a monitoring agency? The government could not reach agreement with the provinces on setting up such an agency, based on either the Food Prices Review Board or the old Prices and Incomes Commission, both of which had the legislative clout to move in and examine the books of companies and organizations that were suspected of going beyond the guidelines. Instead, the government is falling back on the Economic Council of Canada, which was not set up to do this type of work and which does not have the legislative clout to it.
In fact the legislation setting up the Economic Council of Canada included a provision to ensure that it would not duplicate the work of Statistics Canada. The Council can only react to the Statistics Canada figures in the consumer price index. In other words, it can react only after the fact, after the inflationary trend in a particular sector has been identified by Statistics Canada. In terms of an inherent weakness in monitoring during the post controls period, that was not bad enough. This agency does not have labour representation. The Canadian Labour Congress withdrew from it a couple of years ago. That brings up the whole business of co-operation, in order to bring in a post control strategy of voluntary restraints.
Obviously there cannot be cooperation without consultation with labour. Now we know that following the first ministers' conference, and the face-saving move by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in establishing the Economic Council of Canada as a monitoring agency, there was in fact no consultation with CLC on a post controls strategy. There was no consultation with the group in this country which is the aggrieved group representing labour. As a result of the work of

the Anti-Inflation Board and the legislation setting it up, there is not a working person in Canada who does not feel he has been badly used by the Board, because his wages have been controlled while prices have been escalating and allowed to continue to rise. Yet there was no cooperation whatsoever, no move to obtain the cooperation of organized labour.
The other day in Quebec one of the commissioners of the Anti-Inflation Board predicted that controls would have to be reimposed. If the truth were known, I suspect that is a very important part of the government's strategy, the reimposition of controls. He identified the reasons for that. He indicated that most of the wage settlements over the past few years have openers in them for January of next year, in anticipation of controls coming off. With inflation running at 8.8 per cent annually, and showing no signs of improving, we expect labour to operate within voluntary constraint guidelines of 6 per cent! That is a ridiculous expectation.
The budget referred to a reduction in provincial sales taxes. It is the major stimulator for the economy in the budget. I will not deal with the controversy surrounding the measure of consultation with the provinces, or more precisely, the lack of it. One major item which is not covered by retail sales taxes in any of the provinces is food. If one looks at the consumer price index, which was released this week for last month, he will find the food component went up by 1.4 per cent. It has to get worse. As the dollar goes down, the price of imported vegetables and produce goes up.
Yesterday the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) announced a new dairy policy, which means an increase in the price of most Canadian dairy products. A week or so prior to the latest round of ad hoc reactions to the dairy situation and this annual policy statement, the government decided to remove the consumer subsidy on the price of powdered skim milk. This will result in the government saving $13 million in its budget. Is that a good way to save it? It will be at whose expense? It will be at the expense of the low income earners, fixed income earners, the unemployed, the poor, the native people, and the people of the north who use this product. This will mean the retail price of powdered skim milk will rise by anywhere from 40 per cent to 50 per cent, as a direct result of what the government is doing.
The paradox of all of this is that farm incomes continue to go down. The government will have to react to that situation, given the influence of the Canadian farming community upon the Government of Canada. We can anticipate with certainty that food prices will go even higher, driving up our rate of inflation once again.
Before the summer is out and before the new harvest is in, I predict our rate of inflation will be well in excess of 9 per cent as a result of this push in the price of food. I predict there will be more unrest in the farming community, as farmers demand more and more a greater share, and rightly so, because they have arrived at a point in time today where they are losing money.
April 14, 1978

Of course, the other part of the double whammy is the unemployment situation. We have the second worst performance of western industrialized countries insofar as inflation is concerned, but when you compare our situation with that of the United States, Japan, Germany, France and the United Kingdom in terms of unemployment, our performance is by far the worst. Our unemployment rate of 8.6 per cent is the worst of any of the major industrialized western countries of the world.
If you examine the unemployment figures you find there are some very disturbing features about the statistics. For example, youth unemployment is over 16 per cent, and over 10 per cent of women in the work force are unemployed. That is discounted, of course, by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) because he refers to these people as second income earners. In so doing he denies women who work and the young their opportunity in this supposed land of opportunities.
As the Leader of the Opposition said yesterday, women work in this consumer oriented and inflated society of ours because they have to work, quite apart altogether from their right to do so. Female spouses are working today because it is absolutely essential to family income, and they represent about one third of the female work force.
No one questions that.
Except the Minister of Employment and Immigration.
That is not true.

And the Prime Minister. They both keep trying to discount unemployment figures by talking about these second income earners. We have a number of women in the work force today who are the heads of single parent families who obviously have to work to support their families. Obviously the balance is made up of single women who have to work to support themselves, and the young.
What are we doing to our young people, Mr. Speaker? What kind of a country is this when we have a rate of unemployment among people between the ages of 15 and 24 in excess of 16 per cent? Unfortunately that situation will get worse as the current university college year comes to an end and thousands of young Canadians come into the work force looking for the jobs that are so necessary to finance their education, pay off their student loans, and keep themselves during the period of summer holidays. Many of them are graduating from universities and technical schools, highly skilled and trained for jobs that do not exist. The only response we get from the Prime Minister is let them go elsewhere and look for work.
In my own province the unemployment rate is approaching 17 per cent, seasonally adjusted. I am very cynical of that seasonally adjusted figure because it suggests that seasonal workers do not have to work throughout the year in order to
The Budget-Mr. McGrath
supplement their income. Fishermen, for example, have to find work during the winter to supplement their incomes, as do the tourist workers. If you look at the situation in my province in real terms, the unemployment rate is more like 30 per cent.
I heard the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) talk in this House the other day about sales tax and what the 3 percentage point decrease in that tax meant in a province where the sales tax was increased to 11 per cent from 10 per cent. Of course we have the highest sales tax in the country, and naturally this was a reasonable proposition, and any reasonable person would have to agree with him. This means a great deal to the people in a province where the per capita income is the lowest and unemployment is the highest, and where the per capita cost of living is the highest. In that case any substantial reduction in retail sales tax is of major importance.
Not once during the course of that minister's speech did he make any reference whatsoever to the unemployment situation in the province for which he has a great deal of responsibility as our representative in cabinet. Not once did he refer to the unemployment situation in the Atlantic region as a whole, and not once did he refer to the national unemployment situation. This is incredible when you consider he was brought here especially and hastily by government plane from New York to prop up this weak government on national television when it was discovered last Wednesday that the debates were to be carried live across the country. Somebody forgot to tell the minister during the briefing session on the short flight from New York City to Ottawa that we had an unemployment crisis in this country, or that he in fact has a critical unemployment situation in his own province and his own region.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it one o'clock?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It being one o'clock, I do now leave the chair until two o'clock this afternoon.
At one o'clock the House took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 2 p.m.
Order, please. The hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) has the floor, and he has seven minutes remaining.

Mr. Speaker, I will try and make those seven minutes go by as quickly as possible out of deference to my colleagues opposite. When the House adjourned for lunch I was referring to the intervention-albeit, the flying intervention-of the Secretary of State for External Affairs in this debate last Wednesday. He was brought in especially from New York in order to bolster the sagging image of this government in a debate that was at that particular time being televised live nationally on the CBC. I said, and I repeat, that I found it very strange that my colleague from Newfoundland-

April 14, 1978
The Budget-Mr. McGrath
for whom I have very great respect and with whom I have been associated in politics and in business for many years-could possibly make reference to the province for which he has a great deal of responsibility in terms of Cabinet representation, without making one, single, solitary reference to the number one problem in our province and, indeed, in our country: unemployment.
The minister in not one of his better speeches-on reading it one gets the impression it was a hastily prepared speech; he is a great orator and one of the best speakers of the country-in trying to defend the weak record of this government made reference to our position vis-a-vis the other industrialized countries. He said:
Canada has been recognized internationally by all countries, both developed and developing, as a country which has an excellent record in terms of economic management...
A country which had an excellent record, I might add, in terms of economic management. Then he went on to make a remark about a distinguished officer of this House. I regret that intervention very much. It was out of character for the hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs.
He referred to a nightmare that he had, in which he suddenly found the western industrialized countries, meeting as they are to meet next summer in Bonn to discuss the economies of the western world, and he referred to the President of France, the Prime Minister of Great Britain, the Prime Minister of Japan and the President of the United States, and in the midst of this company who should be in Canada's chair but Joe Who! Presumably he was referring to the Leader of the Opposition. Unfortunately, the minister did not stay in the House very long because, if he had, he would have known, having heard the excellent speech of the Leader of the Opposition yesterday, that here is a man who has the ability not only to give good management to this country, but also to restore Canada's badly tarnished international reputation abroad. When the Leader of the Opposition goes abroad, as he will as the prime minister of this country, he will do so with dignity.
Hear, hear!
And there will be no more sliding down the rails of banisters in London-
He might fall.

-as the Prime Minister did on his first trip abroad as Prime Minister of Canada ten years ago. There will be no more pirouettes like the Prime Minister performed last summer at Buckingham Palace. I was in London with my colleague, the parliamentary secretary to the government House leader at the time. I know he felt a twinge of shame, as I did, to see the leader of our country at Buckingham Palace, with the other distinguished leaders of the western world, acting like a buffoon in the presence of the Queen and of other distinguished statesmen.

There is no doubt in my mind, sir, why Canada's reputation has been tarnished, and why the world no longer has confidence in our ability to manage the economy of this country, with those kinds of shenanigans. It would be better for the Secretary of State for External Affairs to have a dream in which there will be something akin to full employment and equality of opportunity in all parts of this country, in which the war on economic regional disparity would be waged successfully, as it has not been for the past ten years.
The minister himself admitted that a short time ago in Nova Scotia, when he said that the DREE program had not been effective in producing jobs. Perhaps we could all dream. Indeed, we can hope with a reasonable degree of justification and realization that if the Prime Minister has the courage to go to the Governor General and dissolve parliament and take his record to the country, this country will be represented abroad with distinction, with great courage, and great skill by a prime minister heading up a Progressive Conservative government. This will be a government that will, as its number one priority, try to instil some investor confidence in this country.
A Progressive Conservative government will try to stop the flow of capital out of this country. The Secretary of State for External Affairs made no reference to that. He made no reference about efforts to do something for the sagging Canadian dollar which is now supposed to be a floating dollar, but which is in fact sinking out of sight. The sagging dollar is having a direct impact on prices in this country and pushing up the inflationary spiral again. Perhaps the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the senior minister of this government, the senior representative for the Atlantic provinces having the responsibility in this government, certainly for his own province, would, instead of making these negative interventions, try to say something positive in this House for a change-
I regret to inform the hon. member that his allotted time has expired.

speakeroldname: Mr. Maurice Dupras (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish at the outset to join the hon. members on this side who rose before me to express my sincere congratulations and my admiration to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) who was courageous enough to introduce a budget which was welcome in all spheres of Canadian society. It was welcome, Mr. Speaker, by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce as well as by nine provincial premiers. I would like to quote, as an example and as an introduction to my remarks, a communique released by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce the day following the budget speech. I quote:
The Minister of Finance introduced this evening what this chamber considers as a responsible budget.
A little further, in the same communique of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, it says:
April 14, 1978

We are very disappointed by the fact that it is going to be only a temporary cut.
But it is obvious that if we want this cut to have some effect on the economy, to prevent consumers from postponing their purchases, there must be a time limit and this limit was agreed to by nine provincial premiers and the Minister of Finance, who said that it could be six and nine months. The purpose was to encourage Canadian consumers to take advantage of the provisions of the budget and to purchase goods that they would normally have bought later.
To go back to the press release, Mr. Speaker, and I quote:
This budget will bring down inflation at a time when wage and price control are coming off, and that is important.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, it is very important; the Chamber of Commerce understood all the nuances contained in the budget brought down by the Minister of Finance. And the Chamber of Commerce, this time, disagrees with my colleague and friend the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) when it says that in its opinion, contrary to the forecast of the Minister of Finance for an increase in the gross national product of 5 per cent, Canada will do as well as any other member of the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, OECD, and that Canada will increase its GNP by 4.5 per cent. What is important as well, to continue quoting the press release of the Chamber of Commerce, is this:
It is worth mentioning that the budget takes into account regional economic disparities and the Chamber of Commerce fully agrees with the formula selected to finance the sales tax cuts. Let us hope all the provinces will co-operate so that the resulting benefits can reach their citizens.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, a bit further, the Chamber states:
We have also noted the new options being made available to individuals when selecting new investment vehicles for their retirement savings.
Here, Mr. Speaker, we are talking of investments in Canada. And back to the quotation once more:
The expansion of the rules allowing tax deferral on the transfer of farm property from parents to children will eliminate what has been a long standing concern to many of our members.
So that is what the Chamber of Commerce had to say in acceptance of the budget of the Minister of Finance.

But before I go on and deal with the budget, I would like to address myself to the remarks made by the speaker who preceded me, the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) regarding the leader of my party. I think he was referring to a gathering of leaders of heads of governments last year where the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was among leaders of the Commonwealth. I am sure he would miss the great popularity of our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) with the other prime ministers of the Commonwealth. I have often witnessed such admiration for my leader.
While attending a CPA conference within the last few weeks, I met with ministers and prime ministers who told me
The Budget-Mr. Dupras
how fortunate Canada and Canadians are to have this Prime Minister as our leader. I am sure the hon. member for St. John's East does not want me to pursue this. However, if he wishes to have this parliament dissolve, I invite him to try to influence his neighbour, the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), to permit unanimous consent so that this House can deal with an election as soon as possible. [Translation]
Mr. Speaker, the budget is the result of lengthy negotiations and discussions with the Canadian premiers. Earlier today in the House, the Leader of the Opposition and a few other members across the aisle were wondering whether indeed there had been consultations. The Minister of Finance then recalled that as early as October 1977, the premiers were told about those measures which might be considered if there was some degree of acceptance. As explained by the right hon. Prime Minister, most premiers agreed and found that it was a commendable step which would help control unemployment by providing immediate stimulus to the economy.
It has also been suggested that the consultation was not extensive enough, that the finance ministers would have needed a few weeks to take their decision. I do not think the outcome would have been different even if our Minister of Finance had allowed his Quebec counterpart two or three months more to make his decision. It has been shown on several occasions, Mr. Speaker, that the Quebec finance minister is the one who is unable to make a decision.
He does not seem to understand all the fine points of preparing a budget, especially on the national scene. This is why he decided, for instance, not to oppose the proposal of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien). He made no counterproposal and no statement on the proposals submitted to him by the Minister of Finance, and it is only afterwards, the day after the budget speech, that the Quebec finance minister discovered it was something that could be implemented in Quebec, but in his own way and only with considerable changes to the budget proposals.
Mr. Speaker, it is important to understand all the problems that this can represent for us, who must think about the general interest of the whole country and not only of a single province. In this regard, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance has solid support from the Quebec caucus members, and if anyone still has any doubt about this, I can say that our position is based on many facts. With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I would first like to recall certain figures for my colleagues. As concerns the export to other provinces of products made in Quebec, according to available figures Quebec exports to other provinces accounted for 50.5 per cent in 1974 compared with 45.7 per cent in 1967. Let us now examine the importance that the interprovincial market could have for Quebec manufacturers since the budget proposals of Mr. Parizeau seem to neglect this. Quebec producers sell 19 per cent of their products to Ontario alone while only 11 per cent

April 14, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Dupras
of the products made in Ontario are sold in Quebec, and the figures have gone up between 1967 and 1974. If we compare the industrial activities of Quebec as a whole with those of the rest of the country, we find that in 1974, once again, Quebec showed a $1.1 billion surplus in its markets in other provinces. Which industry accounted for this surplus? Mr. Speaker, it was in fact the industries that are called the soft sector, which can be confusing since they are not really soft if we consider the importance of those industries. For instance, our textile shipments to the rest of the country show a surplus of $192 million. The clothing manufacturing industry shows a surplus of $111 million, there is a surplus of $59 million for leather products, a surplus of $503 million for other garments, and a surplus of $134 million for the furniture industry.
Mr. Speaker, I wanted to quote those figures to stress the difficulties that the Quebec industry could face if the budget submitted by the provincial minister were passed. To understand the importance of the Quebec market, let us examine, for instance, the Quebec products consigned to Ontario and the other provinces. If the sales tax on furniture is removed, we would perhaps expect this to affect all the production in Quebec. That is not so. It would affect only 56 per cent of the furniture industry because the rest of the production, or 44 per cent, is exported outside the province. As concerns the leather industry, 42 or 43 per cent of the production is exported. In the textile industry, 43 per cent is exported. In the clothing manufacturing industry, nearly 40 per cent of the production is exported, Mr. Speaker. Will the budget proposals of the Quebec finance minister enable furniture manufacturers to sell more furniture outside Quebec? Or will there be an increase in the 55 or 56 per cent of production now sold in Quebec to justify a budget separate from the national budget? Or are the provisions of the provincial budget going to encourage buyers from outside the province, those who buy our leather and textile products, to stimulate the industry in the province of Quebec?
This morning, during the question period, the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) emphasized the outlandishness of such an attitude. It destroys the industry in the province of Quebec and stifles its growth by raising a tariff barrier and preventing a certain sector of retail distribution that needs encouragement in the province of Quebec from benefitting from the provisions of the budget proposed by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien).
So, Mr. Speaker, those aspects have not been studied deeply enough and one of the spokesmen, or indeed the only spokesman for the opposition, the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle), fails to grasp the significance of the problems that might arise from the budget announced last Tuesday by Mr. Parizeau. For instance, he accused hon. members on this side of the House by saying, and I quote:
I heard over the radio this evening a report I hope is true. The report on TV was that a number of members from the Quebec Liberal caucus were meeting this evening to oppose the decision or position taken by the Minister of Finance.

It is absolutely false, Mr. Speaker. And once more he was probably misguided by the media which would be pleased to see a division within the Liberal caucus in the province of Quebec.
That's La Salle!
There is no division!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That's La Salle, as my colleague said and as we say in English, it is wishful thinking.
There is no division!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There is no division! The caucus chairman already indicated, as I said, that the Minister of Finance has the solid backing of his colleagues as far as his budget is concerned.
It is the hon. member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme)!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The caucus chairman reminds me it is the hon. member for Saint-Denis, Mr. Speaker.
There was also that question put by the hon. member for Joliette, asking, and I quote:
I ask my friends from the province of Quebec to have the guts to urge the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) to respect the interests of his own province.
Mr. Speaker, this is something I cannot understand, because no later than this morning reference was made to the Canadian government's generosity to the province of Quebec. Someone said: "Oh, the DREE? Oh yes, in Montreal, the DREE is helping Montreal." They should make up their minds, Mr. Speaker. Is Quebec receiving too much from the federal government, or too little? If the hon. member for Joliette is expressing the views of the opposition, if he in fact is suggesting the Canadian government has not been generous enough to the province of Quebec, well, maybe we should settle this issue. Because I often hear discordant voices, references made to the French Power in Ottawa and all the handouts given the province of Quebec that are not available to other provinces.
He truly betrayed some of his colleagues. It is unfortunate he did not take a few minutes to answer the question put bv my colleague from Bonaventure-Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Bechard) who, having heard such a recital of falsehoods, asked him if he-
... could tell the House the percentage increase in equalization since 1968?
This of course involves payments to the province of Quebec.
I did not compute any Figures, but if my memory does not fail me, this could involve more than $9 billion for 1977, while the figure was $300 million in 1968. Certainly this is a truly significant increase.
There may be different views on the hon. member's party on this side of the House, and among those from the province of Quebec opinions may vary from his, but I would not go so far as to suggest what the hon. member for Joliette indicated about his party when he crossed the House once or twice in
April 14, 1978

1972 and 1973. In any case, Mr. Speaker, I do not think these are words I would like to-
Well, go ahead.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: My colleagues are challenging me to repeat. I would rather not quote the words of the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle). His party favours decentralization, which means weakening the central power. Of course, once again, he cannot see through the scheme of his colleagues who are bent on curtailing the authority of the central government. Let me explain. Of course, if we could reduce the taxation power of the central government, this would benefit two provinces in particular: Alberta and Ontario. As a matter of fact, this would directly affect the equalization payments program. He does not realize that each time the leader and the hon. members of his party advocate decentralization and a reduction of federal powers, they are in fact talking about this program. The main reason why they want to take some of the taxation power away from the central government is to stop equalization payments not only for the province of Quebec, but also for the Atlantic provinces. He has not yet seen through his colleagues' guile and his leader's intention to cut down on the tax power of the central government.
Which leader?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Someone asks, "Which leader?"
They do not have any.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
They may have two to date. There is one who refused to give unanimous consent yesterday so that we could all start campaigning and live up to the mandate Canadian voters gave us in 1974. His refusing unanimous consent is hard to understand. Does this mean the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) is apprehensive about the next campaign? Or is it his contention that the present government is doing so well now that its mandate should be extended? Those questions are worth asking. Anyway, in the Province of Quebec as in most of the other provinces, Canadians support this government. We had evidence of that. People appreciated the government's action when, for example, we introduced compensation payments for oil products, which allowed the Eastern consumers in Quebec, the Maritimes, the Atlantic provinces, the province of my hon. friend from St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), to buy oil at Canadian prices. And that does credit to the generosity and understanding of the people in Alberta. I say the same thing in the province of Quebec, Mr. Speaker. This is further evidence of the great benefits of Canadian confederation: a part of the country, a part of the population is willing to provide temporary assistance to another which does not enjoy similar economic benefits.
All the same, this program was first endorsed by the people in Alberta, by their government, to the benefit not only of the Atlantic provinces but of Quebec as well. The figures which were released this morning suggest that by the end of 1978, the province of Quebec will have received $3 billion under the petroleum compensation program. That is quite an amount of
The Budget-Mr. Dupras
money which not only helped people who drive their children to school or to deliver the goods they manufacture but which has contributed to keep our industry competitive, the agri-food industry which is so sick in the province of Quebec and elsewhere, and all eastern industries which have enjoyed a Canadian price as well as the rest of the country.
There are also all the Quebec-Canada programs under which agreements have been entered into with the province of Quebec. I refer more often to the province of Quebec that to other provinces, because I am trying to make my colleague from Joliette (Mr. La Salle) aware of the advantages of the Canadian Confederation. First of all, he is not convinced of that and I would ask him to commend the generous policy of the Canadian government to his colleagues in his party. That is his weakest point. Indeed, he does not manage to uphold the generosity, the openness of mind shown by the Trudeau government for the economic development of the province of Quebec.
I said a few moments ago that agreements representing investments of $200 or $300 million for the province of Quebec have just been signed. These agreements provide for road construction, the creation of parks to stimulate the tourist industry and a set of other measures which I hope will help eradicate the unemployment that plagues mainly Quebec. One could have foreseen, Mr. Speaker, that following the election of a separatist party in 1976, unemployment would strike very hard in my province. No matter how much money the federal government may inject in industry and the public sector for job creation, if the provincial government does all it can, through ill-advised measures, to thwart economic development, there is not much we can do. It seems also that people are encouraged to refuse the kind of work only people from foreign countries, mainly the Caribbean islands, are prepared to do.
Also, Mr. Speaker, if the current slide of the Canadian dollar is deplored by several sectors of our economy, I know of some industries in my riding that are pleased with it. Of course, I would not say that the dollar must stay low or under the 90 cents level compared to the U.S. dollar. But I dare not think of the problems and the unemployment we would have if the Canadian dollar had not been devaluated. In fact, the dollar has not been devaluated, but was subject to the law of supply and demand, and the value of the dollar today, as the Prime Minister pointed out during the question period this morning, is based on the productivity and performance of the Canadian economy.
This allows Quebec industries, some in particular such as fine paper, to recover the markets lost during the strike in the fine paper industry in 1976. This also allows other industries to develop business in the U.S. and in Europe with the hope of retaining such business when the dollar regains its true value which, when compared to the U.S. dollar, is certainly not 100 cents to the dollar. But in the short term, Mr. Speaker, this had definite advantages for Canadian products in that it promotes our exports and job creation.

April 14, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Dupras
Naturally, there are other causes for the fluctuations of the dollar, if one considers, for example, the performance of the tourist industry in Canada, with a deficit of almost $2 billion in 1977, and this could double in a few years if drastic measures are not taken. Mr. Speaker, we should be very happy with the provisions contained in the budget which will indeed help promote the tourist industry.
This leads me to consider the provision contained in the Quebec provincial budget which removes the 8 per cent tax on hotel rooms. The budget brought down by the Minister of Finance aimed at stimulating the economy and creating jobs. The removal of the 8 per cent tax on hotel rooms will only attain those aims in a few years. Allow me to explain, Mr. Speaker. The tourist industry has suffered, especially in Montreal and in Quebec City, from the lack of major conventions. As we all know, conventions are prepared years in advance so that the people who will be holding conventions in 1980 and 1981 have already signed agreements and made reservations either in North America or in Europe. So this tax cut is only window-dressing, because if you look at the facts, it is very impressive, as it will not really prompt Canadians to visit the province of Quebec unless other corrective action is taken and other measures adopted.
There are two other things, Mr. Speaker, which I could say about the Quebec budget, since they are trying by that new scheme to undermine the strong conviction held by the Canadian people that the Canadian confederation is really working well for all Canadians throughout the country. More than ever in Quebec, the people have such a conviction, as I realized Wednesday last, Mr. Speaker, at my nomination meeting. My fellow citizens, my constituents, are looking to the Canadian government which they consider as their own, with which they can hold a dialogue, a government that listens to its electors and the people of the province.
One only has to consider, for example, the treatment given to the Quebec Council of municipalities at its last convention, where all kinds of tactics were used to keep the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) away, because he had indeed developed a credibility with the civic authorities who found out that this federal minister listened to their grievances and tried by every possible means to help them disprove the arguments put forward by the Quebec premier.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to comment briefly on the decision of a distinguished member of the opposition not to seek re-election. It is no wonder that the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies) has decided not to run again.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Why don't you make your choice for Canada and quit too?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I would make the same decision if I were a member of that party. The hon. member for Don Valley can count on my admiration.
Like John Turner and Donald Macdonald.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Macdonald and Basford are doing the same thing.
And Mitchell Sharp.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I know it has not been easy for the hon. member for Don Valley. I know he has had difficulty convincing his colleagues about a few economic matters.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Why don't you partake in public service and quit?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is wishful thinking. I know the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) would like me to quit, but I was re-nominated.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: You are good for comic relief.
Order, please. The hon. parliamentary secretary has the floor.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker. I would like to end my remarks by saying that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) needs help. I know he is seeking help from his provincial colleagues. He has consulted them and tried to learn their views on the budget.

Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition really needs help, and it is not his lack of understanding of the special problems in Quebec nor his support of a separatist budget which will earn him votes in Quebec.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to participate in this debate this afternoon. While training for my profession I was counselled not to depend upon the size of a listening audience but to make my presentation as though the whole world were listening. Today I have the opportunity to speak in this debate. I am not sure how many people will listen to me, but there are certain things I would like to say anyway.
Back in October, 1977, when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) bootlegged a mini-budget into the throne speech debate, the response of this party was that the minister was only tinkering with the system to avoid a full-fledged budget debate. In fact the minister declined to call his mini-budget a budget. He called it an economic statement. Nevertheless, there were some similarities, and perhaps the mini-budget of last October was more like a real budget than the one we are discussing today.
We on this side felt that the minister's response last October to the economic realities of the country was completely inadequate. Since last October whenever we on this side of the House have called for firm and decisive action, the minister's response has been to say that we have to wait until we see the results of the measures introduced last October. We have been told we have to wait until the results of those measures trickle down and it becomes obvious as to the extent to which the

April 14, 1978

proposals are effective. At one point the minister even tried to insult the intelligence of the Canadian people by suggesting that the measures announced by his predecessor, Mr. Macdonald, on March 31, 1977, had not yet taken effect. I suppose if those measures did not take effect, certainly the ones introduced last fall could hardly be expected to produce results today.
The minister has made his first legitimate budget statement in this House, and as my leader pointed out so aptly yesterday, it was the minister's first and last budget. We find ourselves in the same situation we were in previously. The minister has tinkered here and fiddled there, with the same lack of commitment and the same ignorance of economic reality. The same thing happened in March and in October of 1977. It has been said that Nero fiddled while Rome burned, and I think possibly it would be appropriate to say that in this instance Chretien tinkered while Canada tumbled.
Nothing illustrates more the utter bankruptcy of this government's policies than the tumble of the Canadian dollar on the world money markets. This has been more pronounced even since the minister made his budget statement a few evenings ago. The morning after the budget announcement, the dollar sank to a low of 87.57 cents. Then it continued to tumble downward to its current level of 86.79 cents in terms of the U.S. dollar as of noon today. This indicates in a frighteningly dramatic way that the international community of economic experts have no confidence whatever in the government's ability to meet the serious problems facing our nation at present.
While I am on this point may I just say that Canadians should be outraged at the way this government has handled the decline of the dollar. It is bad enough that the dollar has fallen, but in the long slide from its former level to its current level Canadians have lost between $1 billion and $1.5 billion. This is money wasted, and I say Canadians should be outraged. On the one hand, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) says we have a floating dollar, and this was stated again by the Minister of Finance, and on the other hand the Minister of Finance pours $1.5 billion down the drain to keep the dollar from floating. It is precisely this kind of indecision and dishonesty on the part of the government which causes lack of confidence in the Canadian dollar.
I believe it is time the Prime Minister and his government came clean with the Canadian people on this issue: do we have a floating dollar or do we not?
Yes.

If we have a floating dollar, then why go to the trouble of trying to prop it up and, by this means, keep it from floating? Someone said yesterday that the dollar has been floating. It has been sinking until today, and if you want to see it, you have to wear goggles and a snorkle. Perhaps we should consider that. Perhaps it is time to put away the
The Budget-Mr. Patterson
wishy-washy economics of expediency and introduce some basic directional changes.
All of our reputable domestic economic analysts were in agreement prior to the budget's introduction that a complete structural turn-around was necessary in our economic and fiscal policies to restore confidence in our national economy, get the country working again, and stem the tide of spiralling inflation. In this task the minister has failed miserably. All he could do was just to tinker around with it. I think we could say that Macdonald the thumper has been replaced by Chretien the tinker.
I say that structural changes are necessary in this country, but there appears to be no desire on the part of this tired, aging, weak government to put any direction into our national economy. The government has been preoccupied with many other matters, in fact so preoccupied that it has no time or desire to pay attention to the critical economic matters facing us.
I remember that for months the government trumpeted the idea that, after all, the major problem in Canada was national unity and that, if we were to achieve national unity, it was going to be by the implementation of linguistic policies, and everybody had to accept that. The responsibility and the blame were placed upon the English speaking people of this country, and the result was a great deal of resentment. But in later times, when things began to get pretty tough and the Prime Minister came alive, he and some of his ministers began to say that, after all, the most important problem facing Canada was the economy. I am not just sure what they think is the most important problem. The Prime Minister has been too concerned with the language policy and with other matters concerning the contractual link with the European Economic Community. He and his ministers have been determined to change the social structure of Canada and to change the moral values of this nation. They have been too busy with these things to take care of the fundamental problem that confronts us, namely, that if we cannot solve our economic problems we will not have the occasion to take care of our country in the long run.
We come to the conclusion then that after looking at the picture as it has developed, an exodus of supporters of the government has begun, and an exodus of cabinet ministers, which is very significant. My friend, the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Dupras), was talking about the ones who have decided not to run for the Conservative party this time, but I ask him why has John Turner left, why has Paul Hellyer left, why have many others left, such as Don Macdonald, for instance? Were they unimportant individuals? Did they not count in the make-up of the cabinet or in the make-up of the party? Where did they go and why did they go? How can the government go to the people and tell them "return us", when many of their most important, influential and able ministers could not stand it and left?

They are left with their disabled.
4524

April 14, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Patterson

It is quite evident where the lack of confidence is. They just could not see themselves supporting the lack of policies that had characterized this government, so they pulled out and said they were not going to waste their time.
